opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons it's genuinely hard. The first is just the sheer scale of change we're likely to see. If you look at the trends in training compute, we've been scaling up the compute used for the largest training runs by something like four to five times per year. If that continues to 2030, you're talking about models trained with thousands of times more compute than today's frontier systems, and on top of that you have algorithmic progress that effectively multiplies that further. We just don't have a great intuition for what a jump of that magnitude looks like in terms of capabilities.

The second issue is that the relationship between scale and specific capabilities isn't something we understand very well. Scaling laws are quite good at predicting things like the loss, how well a model predicts the next token, but translating that into "can this system do autonomous software engineering" or "can it do scientific research" is much harder. Capabilities on particular tasks can emerge somewhat abruptly, and benchmarks tend to saturate quickly, so we often lack good measuring sticks for the things we actually care about.

And then third, there's a lot of uncertainty about the inputs themselves. Will the scaling continue? That depends on things like whether we can build enough data centers, whether there's enough power, whether chip production keeps up, whether we run out of high-quality data, and whether investors keep being willing to put in tens or hundreds of billions of dollars. Each of those has its own uncertainty, and they compound.

So when I try to think about 2030, I end up with a pretty wide distribution. On one end, you might have systems that are substantially better assistants but still need a lot of human oversight. On the other end, it's quite plausible to me that you get systems that can automate a large fraction of remote work tasks, which would be a really transformative development. I think being honest about that uncertainty is important, but it shouldn't be an excuse for not taking the more dramatic scenarios seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling laws predict loss well, while specific capabilities are harder to predict; it does not say scaling laws inadequately predict benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: It says predicting specific capabilities is harder than predicting loss and that benchmarks can saturate, but does not clearly compare predicting real-world value with predicting benchmark performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think part of it is just that the dynamics here are pretty unusual compared to most technologies we've tried to forecast. With most technologies, you can look at the trajectory of some input, like how much we're spending or how fast the hardware is improving, and you get a reasonably stable mapping from that input to what the thing can actually do. With AI, the mapping between inputs and capabilities is itself something we understand only loosely. We have scaling laws that tell us pretty confidently how loss or perplexity will fall as you add compute and data, but the thing people actually care about is whether a system can do novel mathematics, or autonomously run a research project, or displace a particular kind of worker. And the connection between those downstream capabilities and the quantities we can extrapolate is noisy and sometimes discontinuous. You see benchmarks sitting near zero for years and then saturating in eighteen months.

The second issue is that the inputs themselves are uncertain over that horizon. If you look at the trends over the last decade, training compute has grown something like four or five times per year, and that's been driven by spending growing rapidly, by hardware getting more efficient, and by algorithmic progress that effectively multiplies your compute. Each of those has a plausible story for continuing to 2030 and a plausible story for slowing. Can labs actually mobilize hundreds of billions of dollars for individual training runs? Will there be enough power, enough chips, enough high-quality data? Does the recent shift toward spending compute at inference time, on reasoning, change how much training scale matters? Small differences in those growth rates compound enormously over five or six years. The difference between compute growing at three x a year and five x a year by 2030 is something like two orders of magnitude, and that's the gap between a fairly incremental world and a very strange one.

And then the third thing, which I think people underweight, is feedback effects. If AI systems become genuinely useful for AI research, for writing the code, running the experiments, finding the algorithmic improvements, then the rate of progress stops being exogenous. It starts depending on the capabilities you're trying to forecast. That makes the whole thing much harder to reason about, because you're no longer extrapolating a trend, you're trying to model a system where the output feeds back into the input. So I tend to hold fairly wide distributions. I think there's a real chance 2030 looks like a modestly better version of today, and a real chance it looks like something that's hard to recognize, and I don't think we have the tools yet to narrow that very much.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling laws predict loss and perplexity, while downstream capabilities are difficult to infer and benchmarks can change abruptly. It does not clearly identify scaling laws as inadequate for predicting benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: It contrasts relatively predictable loss or perplexity with harder-to-forecast capabilities people care about, such as doing novel mathematics, conducting research, or displacing workers.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is that we’re trying to predict capabilities through several layers of uncertainty. There’s how much compute people will use, how much progress we’ll make in algorithms, and how effectively we’ll be able to use data. But even if you knew all of those things, you’d still need to translate them into what a system can actually do.

We can sometimes predict improvements in training loss fairly well. It’s much harder to say what those improvements mean for something like conducting research or reliably completing a project that takes a human several weeks. We don’t have a very good theory connecting those things.

And by 2030, progress might also depend on how much AI itself contributes to developing better AI. That creates a feedback loop whose strength is quite uncertain. So you can have reasonably grounded expectations about some of the inputs and still have a very wide range of plausible outcomes for capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says training-loss improvements can sometimes be predicted, but it does not identify inadequate scaling laws or benchmark-performance prediction as the issue.

r002.rationale: It says translating training-loss improvements into practical abilities such as conducting research or completing a multiweek project is much harder, clearly distinguishing measurable performance from real-world capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is that we’re extrapolating through several layers of uncertainty. We can make fairly informed guesses about how much compute will be available and how much companies might spend on training. But translating those inputs into capabilities is much harder. Even if you can predict a model’s performance on its training objective, that doesn’t tell you straightforwardly whether it can carry out a research project or reliably do someone’s job.

There’s also uncertainty about algorithmic progress and how these systems will be used. A model on its own might struggle with a task, but give it tools, more time to think, and a way to check its work, and it might perform much better. Those improvements are difficult to anticipate several years in advance.

So I think we can say useful things about the direction of progress, but there’s a very wide range of plausible outcomes for 2030. The uncertainty is especially large for tasks that require sustained, reliable performance over long periods.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty in translating training compute and objective performance into capabilities, but does not identify inadequate scaling laws for predicting benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: It says predicting model performance on a training objective does not straightforwardly predict whether a system can do research or reliably perform someone’s job, conveying that real-world capability is harder to predict than benchmark-like performance.
